## data prep

The dataset is loaded and curated. We remove repetitions where adult = 0 as well as all rows containing NAs. This is justified because we believe that adult mortality is linked to issues occurring during installation rather than a response from the plant. Since adult death directly affects fecundity measures, keeping these cases would introduce substantial bias.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| results: hide
data250_afabae_00 <- read.csv("../../../../../../01.data/2023_screen_specifics_251genotypes/02.aphis_fabae_on_faba_collection/aphis_fabae_fecundity_on_faba_collection_2024-04-02.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE, sep = ",") %>%  
  mutate(ivip = as.factor(ivip)) %>% 
  mutate(session = as.factor(session)) 

data250_afabae_01 <- data250_afabae_00 %>% filter(!is.na(larvae_total_number))
data250_afabae_01$ivip <- droplevels(data250_afabae_01$ivip)

data250_afabae_02<- data250_afabae_01 %>% filter(adult_alive != "0") #remove if no adult
data250_afabae_02$ivip <- droplevels(data250_afabae_02$ivip)

data250_afabae_02$ivip <-as.factor(data250_afabae_02$ivip)

```

Once we have removed the NAs and all rows for which we don't have an adult, we can still make adjustments to the dataset. We can remove outliers to ensure that our distribution approaches a normal distribution, and we can also filter out genotypes based on a threshold for the minimum number of repetitions required to keep a genotype. We have 3 methods to handle outliers: 1)keep the outliers; 2)remove manually the outliers based on biological reasons; 3) use the interquartile range method (IQR) to remove all data outside a specific range.

The goal of this script is to study how our model reacts to changes in the outlier removal method and the minimum number of repetitions required to retain a genotype.

in the folowing loop we varry two parameters, i the minimal number of reps for the genotypes and the outlier filtering method.


## function to calculate all metric used to compare filters
```{r}
analyze_filtered_data <- function(data, i, filter_name) {
  data <- data %>%
    group_by(ivip) %>%
    filter(n() >= i) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    droplevels()

  if (nrow(data) < 5 || nlevels(data$ivip) < 2) {
    return(NULL)  # skip iterations with too little data
  }

  NGEN <- nlevels(data$ivip)
  n_after <- nrow(data)

  # Fit the model
  mod <- lmer(larvae_total_number ~ ivip + (1|session/block), data = data)
  residuals_values <- residuals(mod)
  RMSE <- sqrt(mean(residuals_values^2))
  shapiro_res <- shapiro.test(residuals_values)$p.value
  shapiro <- shapiro.test(data$larvae_total_number)$p.value

  # Heritability model
  mod_h2 <- lmer(larvae_total_number ~ (1 | ivip) + (1 | session), data = data)
  estimates <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mod_h2))
  genetic_variance <- estimates$vcov[1]
  residual_variance <- estimates$vcov[3]
  nbE <- nlevels(data$session)
  H2 <- genetic_variance / (genetic_variance + (residual_variance / nbE))

  return(data.frame(
    filter = filter_name, i = i, RMSE = RMSE, n_after = n_after,
    H2 = H2, shapiro = shapiro, shapiro_res = shapiro_res, NGEN = NGEN
  ))
}
```

## analyse of the filtered datasets
```{r}

# Initialize an empty data frame to store results
results <- data.frame(x = numeric(0), i = numeric(0), RMSE = numeric(0), 
                       n_after = numeric(0), H2=numeric(0),shapiro=numeric(0),shapiro_res=numeric(0),NGEN=numeric(0), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)


###filter based on IQR
    # Calculate IQR and bounds for outlier removal
    IQR_value <- IQR(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number)
    lower_bound <- quantile(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number, 0.25) - 1.5 * IQR_value
    upper_bound <- quantile(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number, 0.75) + 1.5 * IQR_value
    filter ="IQR"
    # Filter out outliers
    data_iqr <- data250_afabae_02[data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number >= lower_bound & data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number <= upper_bound, ]
    

for (i in 2:9) {
  res <- analyze_filtered_data(data_iqr, i, filter_name = "IQR")
  if (!is.null(res)) results <- rbind(results, res)
}

for (i in 2:9) {
  res <- analyze_filtered_data(data250_afabae_02, i, filter_name = "no_filter")
  if (!is.null(res)) results <- rbind(results, res)
    }
    

  # Identify the indices of the top 3 highest values
top_3_indices <- order(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
    # View the top 3 highest values
data250_afabae_02[top_3_indices, ] %>% dplyr::select(genotype, ivip, aphid, larvae_total_number)

# Remove the rows with the top 3 highest values
data250_afabae_03 <- data250_afabae_02[-top_3_indices, ]

data_manual<- data250_afabae_03 %>% filter(larvae_total_number != "0") 

for (i in 2:9) {
  res <- analyze_filtered_data(data_manual, i, filter_name = "Manual_filter")
  if (!is.null(res)) results <- rbind(results, res)
}

print(results)
```
Based on these results it seems appropriate to select the IQR filter as it yield best heritability, lower RMSE and more normal data.


We now need to visualize the data we generated from the IQR filter to choose the best value for i (minimal number of repetitions to keep a genotype in the analysis). The code will remove all genotypes for which we have less than i repetitions. The choice or i is complex as a higher value for i means that we have less genotypes in the GWAS but the genotypes we have have more repetition. However with a lower value for i we have more genotypes in the annalysis but some will have low number of repetition. Our objective is to find the optimal value to maximise the GWAS power without adding too much noise. We metrics we use to choose based on overall number of genotypes, total number of data points, RMSE and heritability.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
write.csv(x = results, 
          file = "filter_annalysis.csv", 
          quote = F, row.names = F)

```

Based on these first results it appears that IQR is the best filtering option. We still need to determine the best value for i.

```{r}
# Initialize an empty data frame to store results
results <- data.frame(x = numeric(0), i = numeric(0), RMSE = numeric(0), 
                       n_after = numeric(0), H2=numeric(0),shapiro=numeric(0),shapiro_res=numeric(0),NGEN=numeric(0), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)


for (i in 2:9) {
  ###filter based on IQR
    # Calculate IQR and bounds for outlier removal
    IQR_value <- IQR(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number)
    lower_bound <- quantile(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number, 0.25) - 1.5 * IQR_value
    upper_bound <- quantile(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number, 0.75) + 1.5 * IQR_value
    filter ="IQR"
    # Filter out outliers
    data <- data250_afabae_02[data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number >= lower_bound & data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number <= upper_bound, ]
    
    
    data <- data %>%
      group_by(ivip) %>%           # Group by genotype
      filter(n() >= i) %>%             # Keep only groups with i or more repetitions
      ungroup() 
    
    
    data$ivip <- droplevels(data$ivip)
    
    NGEN<-nlevels(data$ivip)
    
   
 
    
    
    # Number of rows after removing outliers
    n_after <- nrow(data)
    

    
    # Fit the model
    mod <- lmer(larvae_total_number ~ ivip + (1|session/block), data = data)
    
    # Extract fitted values and residuals
    fitted_values <- fitted(mod)
    residuals_values <- residuals(mod)
    
    # Perform the Shapiro-Wilk test
    shapiro_result <- shapiro.test(residuals_values)
    
    # Print the p-value (this is your quantification of normality)
    shapiro_res <- shapiro_result$p.value
    
    # Perform the Shapiro-Wilk test
    shapiro_result <- shapiro.test(data$larvae_total_number)
    
    # Print the p-value (this is your quantification of normality)
    shapiro <- shapiro_result$p.value
    
    
    # Calculate RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)
    RMSE <- sqrt(mean(residuals_values^2))
    
    # Fit the model with a fixed formula
    mod_h2 <- lmer(larvae_total_number ~ (1 | ivip) + (1 | session), data = data)
    
    # Get the variance components
    estimates <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mod_h2))
    
    # Extract the relevant variance components
    genetic_variance <- estimates$vcov[1]
    residual_variance <- estimates$vcov[3]  # Adjust based on the placement of residual variance
    
    nbE <-nlevels(data$session)
    
    # Calculate heritability (h2)
    H2 <- genetic_variance / (genetic_variance + (residual_variance / nbE))
    

    # Store the results in the data frame
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(filter = filter, i = i, RMSE = RMSE, n_after = n_after, H2 = H2, shapiro = shapiro, shapiro_res = shapiro_res, NGEN=NGEN))
}


```

We now need to visualize the data we generated to choose the best filter

```{r}

ggplot(results, aes(x = i, y = NGEN)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(1,13,1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,250)) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = NGEN), arrow = T) +
  labs(x = "minimal number of rep per genotype", y = "N genotypes")

y<-as.vector(results$NGEN)
x<-as.vector(results$i)

# Compute slope (finite differences)
slope <- diff(y) / diff(x)

# To align slopes with x-values, use midpoints
x_mid <- (x[-1] + x[-length(x)]) / 2

# Plot slope (derivative)
plot(x_mid, slope, type = "b", col = "red", main = "Numerical Derivative (Slope)",
     ylab = "Slope", xlab = "minimal number of rep per genotype")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray", lty = 2)  # reference line for zero slope



```

It can be hard to read the relation between Genotype number and i. Therefore it is helpfull to plot the slop (the value is the difference between number of genotype with i and i + 1). From 2 to 5 the slope is progressive then we start genotypes with a higher rate.

```{r}
x<-as.vector(results$i)

# Compute slope (finite differences)

# To align slopes with x-values, use midpoints
x_mid <- (x[-1] + x[-length(x)]) / 2

# Plot slope (derivative)
plot(x_mid, slope, type = "b", col = "red", main = "Numerical Derivative (Slope)",
     ylab = "Slope", xlab = "minimal number of repetition per genotype")
```

the lowest value for RMSE is with i=4. 

```{r}
ggplot(results, aes(x = i, y = n_after)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(1,13,1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1800)) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = n_after), arrow = T) +
  labs(x = "minimal number of rep per genotype", y = "total number of rep") +
  ggtitle("total number of observation depending on the number of repetitions")

y<-as.vector(results$n_after)
x<-as.vector(results$i)

# Compute slope (finite differences)
slope <- diff(y) / diff(x)

# To align slopes with x-values, use midpoints
x_mid <- (x[-1] + x[-length(x)]) / 2

# Plot slope (derivative)
plot(x_mid, slope, type = "b", col = "red", main = "Numerical Derivative (Slope)",
     ylab = "Slope", xlab = "minimal number of rep per genotype")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray", lty = 2)  # reference line for zero slope

```

The total number or repetition is the total number of line in our dataset (the number of genotypes x number of repetition per genotype). This metric slowly decrease as i increase. For a i value of 2 to 4 decrease we lose only few repetition, then from 6 to 9 the slope increase and the rate of repetition loss increase.

```{r}
ggplot(results, aes(x = i, y = H2)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 13, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.5)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "minimal number of rep per genotype",
    y = "H2"
  ) +
  ggtitle("H2 depending on the number of repetitions")


y<-as.vector(results$H2)
x<-as.vector(results$i)

# Compute slope (finite differences)
slope <- diff(y) / diff(x)

# To align slopes with x-values, use midpoints
x_mid <- (x[-1] + x[-length(x)]) / 2

# Plot slope (derivative)
plot(x_mid, slope, type = "b", col = "red", main = "Numerical Derivative (Slope)",
     ylab = "Slope", xlab = "minimal number of rep per genotype")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray", lty = 2)  # reference line for zero slope

```

the highest heritabilty are obtained with i=2, 3 or 4. Heritability then progresivelly decrease as we increase the minimal number of repetitions required.


Based on all the metrics presented here it seems that a value of 4 or less would be optimal. choosing 5 could be tempting as we don't lose too much heritability and we don't gain too much RMSE but due to the already low number of genotypes reducing the genotype loss is our priority. However we think that 4 is the minimal number of acceptable repetitions. Going lower to 4 would be quite risky especially since we know that our phenotypes is quite variable. Therefore we choose to keep 4 as the ideal value for i. In the next steps we will conduct GWAS on dataset filterd with a i value of 4, 5 and 6. This is intended to make sure that the choice of i does not change the GWAS pics the detect, however we will only use the GWAS pics from the dataset with i=4.


We know have to make sure this filtering does not include some bias. We want to asses this throught 2 key points, the resistance level and the genetic cluster.


```{r}
# -------------------------------
# 1. IQR filtering
# -------------------------------
IQR_value <- IQR(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number)
lower_bound <- quantile(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number, 0.25) - 1.5 * IQR_value
upper_bound <- quantile(data250_afabae_02$larvae_total_number, 0.75) + 1.5 * IQR_value

data <- data250_afabae_02 %>%
  filter(larvae_total_number >= lower_bound,
         larvae_total_number <= upper_bound)

# -------------------------------
# 2. Keep ivip with ≥4 repetitions
# -------------------------------
data_afabae_4 <- data %>%
  group_by(ivip) %>%
  filter(n() >= 4) %>%
  ungroup()

# -------------------------------
# 3. Identify ivip NOT kept
# -------------------------------
ivip_not_in_4 <- setdiff(unique(data$ivip), unique(data_afabae_4$ivip))
data_removed <- data %>% filter(ivip %in% ivip_not_in_4)

# -------------------------------
# 4. Boxplot with removed ivip in red
# -------------------------------
ggplot(data, aes(x = "", y = larvae_total_number)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = data_removed,
             aes(x = "", y = larvae_total_number),
             color = "red",
             size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of larvae_total_number",
       subtitle = "Red points = ivip removed (<4 repetitions)") +
  theme_minimal()

# -------------------------------
# 5. Table of removed ivip with genetic cluster
# -------------------------------
info_cluster <- read.csv("../../../../../../00.info/11.infos_genotypes/morphological_phenotlogical_data_faba_collection_PeaMUST_with_genet_cluster.csv")

ivip_removed_cluster_table <- data.frame(ivip = ivip_not_in_4) %>%
  left_join(info_cluster, by = "ivip")

ivip_removed_cluster_table

# -------------------------------
# 6. Cluster summary table
# -------------------------------
# Keep only non-empty, non-NA cluster_name
ivip_with_cluster <- data %>%
  distinct(ivip) %>%
  left_join(info_cluster, by = "ivip") %>%
  filter(!is.na(cluster_name), cluster_name != "")

cluster_summary <- ivip_with_cluster %>%
  group_by(cluster_name) %>%
  summarise(
    n_original = n(),
    n_removed = sum(ivip %in% ivip_not_in_4)
  ) %>%
  arrange(cluster_name)

cluster_summary
```

based on these results it does not seems that we have a cluster or resistance level bias
